articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) recently hosted a party to thank donors for their contributions to the Piedmont Aquatic Center. During the event, President Patty Dunlap announced that PBF’s Spring Campaign will support the City in creating a new Nature Play Area in Piedmont Park. Karen Sullivan, PBF President during the pool campaign, recounted the foundation’s efforts to make the aquatic center a reality. PBF was an early endorser of Measure UU, and Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen credited this support as crucial to the bond measure’s passage. PBF contributed a total of $239,000 to the project, specifically earmarked for the drought-tolerant and native landscaping that now graces the Aquatics Center. For mer Mayor Valer ie Matzger and Piedmont Park and Projects Manager Nancy Kent spoke about the importance of using low-water California native plants. They led donor groups around the center to view the collection and shared plans for the upcoming Nature Play Area which will be in Piedmont’s Main Park adjacent to new swings. This project will transform an under-used section into a vibrant outdoor learning space featuring climbing logs, natural play elements and hands-on spaces where children can engage with the outdoors in meaningful ways. A PBF brochure will be arriving at every Piedmont home soon with an envelope to support the Nature Play Area or other ongoing initiatives, including the Dearing Memorial. Contributions can also be mailed to City Hall (120 Vista Ave, Piedmont, CA 94611) or made through the PBF website: www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org. Valerie Matzger shows Aquatic Center native plants to PBF donors. Photo by Sharon Hom

articles.text: Did you know that Monday, June 8, is World Oceans Day? As we head into Summer, which often means spending time at the beach, I have a challenge for us. How much garbage can we prevent from ending up on our beaches, in our oceans, and in other waterways? I’m a rising senior at PHS and I have a summer challenge that is related to my Girl Scout Gold Award Project. I’m a sailor and sailing instructor, and I spend a ton of time on the water thinking about our oceans. Many of us are familiar with California Coastal Cleanup Day, which will be September 19 this year. Beach cleanups like this and other less well-known beach and waterway cleanups are incredibly important for helping clean up coastal garbage. Ocean and beach garbage is a huge problem — millions of tons of plastic and garbage enter our marine ecosystems every year. But wouldn’t it be great if we could prevent garbage from ending up there in the first place? What if we focused more attention on making sure that trash cans at beaches and waterways aren’t allowed to overflow? When trash cans overflow, lightweight plastics — bags, wrappers, cups and straws — get blown into the water and end up in the ocean and surrounding ecosystems. Preventing trash can overflow may not seem like an important solution at first, but it is one of the most immediate and impactful solutions that individual citizens can contribute to and have control over. Permanent solutions to the overflowing trash can issue is going to be slow and complicated, because it will require coordination between local governments, parks, and community organizations to increase the frequency of trash collection or expand the number, size, or design of trashcans at popular, highly used coastal areas. While I’m working on making that happen, there is a much simpler, immediate solution that each one of us can make happen. We can pledge to bring our own trash home with us from each beach outing. Each piece of plastic or garbage that is properly contained in a home trash can is a piece of garbage that doesn’t get blown into our oceans, doesn’t enter the food chain of marine life, doesn’t wash up on shore, and doesn’t break down into the microplastics that are found in our oceans. I hope you will join me for an early celebration of World Oceans Day by signing up for my Ocean Garbage Prevention Challenge, and pledge to take action - either by helping prevent garbage from ending up in our oceans, or by helping clean it up once it’s there. Please spread the word! If we can prevent more garbage from entering our oceans, we will have even less garbage to collect on California Coastal Cleanup Day on September 19. –See you at the Beach! https://forms.gle/NeG7uqSkPiTSkG

articles.text: A car crashed into Broadway Terrace Nursery on May 28. From the parking lot, the vehicle impacted the side of the nursery, going through the outside wall and damaging the indoor plant area. One person was injured in the accident. Due to the damage sustained in the accident, the nursery’s indoor section is closed temporarily. The impacted wall is now covered with plywood to cover the hole left by the car. “The safety of our customers and staff is our priority. Our indoor plant section sustained damage and will remain closed while we assess the space and confirm it is safe,” said Jenny Feinberg, the recent new owner of Broadway Terrace Nursery and Yarrow Nursery This is the second time this year a car has crashed into the Broadway Terrace Nursery. The first incident occurred during the nursery’s opening week in February. In that incident, a car crashed through the nursery, breaking two walls and destroying part of the indoor area. Feinberg spent the next month rebuilding the indoor space. Broadway Terrace Nursery remains open and visitors can access the outdoor plant section while the indoor area undergoes repairs. To learn more about the nursery, readers can visit the website: https://www.broadwayterracenursery.com/. articles.text: Marshall and Lorenzo are two best friends determined to make the most of every day together! Lorenzo, just 4 months old, is the outgoing adventurer of the pair. Friendly, confident, and endlessly curious, he’s always ready to investigate a new toy or follow his people around the house. He approaches life with enthusiasm—whether he’s batting a toy across the floor, learning a new trick for treats, or flopping over to ask for pets. Seven-month-old Marshall is equally affectionate and enjoys soft pets and snuggling close. His easygoing nature makes hearts melt left and right, and when he’s feeling mischievous, you’ll find him in a friendly wrestling match, or instigating a game of chase with his best buddy! Marshall and Lorenzo are almost always side by side—grooming one another, bird-watching, cuddling, and even eating together. articles.text: On Wednesday, June 3, Piedmont’s school board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting in the District Office Board Room, 760 Magnolia Avenue, at 7:00 p.m. This meeting occurs on the eve of the last day of school and will include a first reading on changes to next year’s student cell phone policy. The Mobile Communications Device policy will seek to get rid of the phone hotels in each high school classroom but it will allow high schoolers to use a non-smart phone or “dumbphone” with talk and text features only, during non-instruction times. “TK-12 students shall have their mobile devices, including phones, smartphones, smart devices, and any other personal internet-connected device turned off, or silenced, and stored during the instructional day while on campus. High school students may access a “feature” or “dumbphone” that has talk and text only (no apps or camera) during non-instr uctional/classroom times throughout the school day,” the first reading of the policy currently reads. The board will also adjust its board meeting conduct policy for public speakers, “In general, individual speakers will be allowed 2 minutes, 30 seconds to address the Board on each agenda item and 1 minute, 30 seconds to address the Board on any nonagenda item. The Board will limit the total time for public input on non-agenda items to 30 minutes and on each item to 20 minutes,” the policy reads. The board also plans to levy a 2% increase to the Measure G flat-rate per-parcel tax. This would increase the tax to $3,111 per parcel, a $61 increase. The board points to the consumer price index which is projected to increase by 3.76% in the coming year. The new proposed Measure H, if approved by voters in the June 2 election, would not replace Measure G until 2027-28. The first presentation of the evening will recognize retiring Certificated and Classified staff. The second presentation will review the current Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP), after the completion of the second year of its three year duration. The LCAP presentation will give highlights of how the plan is meeting its four goals and offer potential changes. articles.text: Adelaide Lee and Maya Sweeney, Havens 5th graders, were named top 10 finalists in the 2026 “Celebrate America” Creative Writing Contest. Sweeney and Lee submitted their entries as part of a writing assignment for Katy Levin’s class and were selected out of hundreds of submissions from fifth graders across Northern California. Since 1998 the contest has been sponsored by the American Immigration Council and the American Immigration Lawyers Association of Northern California. Students were asked to write an essay reflecting on the themes “Why I’m glad immigrants are part of our communities and nation” and “What does it mean to be a welcoming nation?” A Special Award Ceremony was held on May 13 at the Chinese American Citizens Alliance building in San Francisco for the top 10 finalists. Haram Naseer Ahmed, a student from Corte Madera’s The Cove School, was awarded first place in the region and will have his essay judged with winners from across the country for the national grand prize. Lee and Sweeney received trophies, medals and a cash prize for their essays, as did Ms. Levin and all the teachers of winning students. articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council was well-represented at the Scouting America National Annual Meeting held in Dallas in mid-May. Attendees included Kate Benson, former Piedmont Scout Executive and now National Director of Cub Scouts; Glyn Burge, Piedmont Council President; Glen Tripp, Piedmont Council Commissioner; Rob James, Council Territory Leadership and Governance Lead; Rick Clark, Council Territory Finance Lead; Anne-Marie Lamarche, National Executive Board Member; and Wes Smith, National Executive Board Member. At the meeting, Scouting leaders from across the country heard an ambitious plan to double membership nationwide from 877,000 to 2,000,000 youth. Scouting America National Chair Ricky Mason emphasized the need for Scouting to help kids “learn, fail, grow, and become leaders” while spending less time on screens. “Scouting sets kids on a path of learning, achieving, and respecting and leading others. It gives them true grit, while having the most fun and adventure possible,” said Mason. Roger Krone, President and CEO, shared that youth safety and membership growth remain the organization’s top priorities and that the long-running bankruptcy case tied to sexual abuse claims has officially concluded after the Supreme Court declined to hear a final challenge earlier this year. Piedmont continues to have a strong presence in national leadership, with Anne-Marie Lamarche and Wes Smith serving on the National Executive Board. A highlight of the event came during the Silver Antelope luncheon, where Piedmont’s own Rob James received the prestigious Silver Antelope Award. Piedmont art students shine in AP Art Show By Jay Russell On Monday, May 18, Advanced Placement (AP) art students from Piedmont and Millennium High displayed the best of their work in the Alan Harvey Theater foyer. Each AP student displayed at least five of their drawings, paintings or 3-D design pieces. Milana Milner’s art explored her memories through color and pattern drawings of familiar architecture. She used unnaturally bright colors to illustrate the lens of a kid growing up. “My work invokes feelings of nostalgia through painting on objects that I associate with childhood memories. In escapism through painting on objects, I take myself and the viewer away from societal pressures and societal expectations through invoking childhood memories,” said Enzo Ong. Lucas Smolko’s work accentuates landscapes using composition and color schemes. “Studying composition assisted me in creating aesthetic compositions such as leading lines, rule of thirds, and other composition Audrey Dickinson schemes,” said Smolko. These pieces will serve as cornerstones for the AP artists’ portfolio of 10 pieces presented to The College Board. “Influenced by my memories and the sensory power of music, I use candid, immersive compositions to elevate simple scenes into reflective spaces,” said Leighton Mand. The art gallery served as a powerful entry way to the theater, which concurrently hosted the Senior Awards, and as a first stop to the high school’s open house. articles.text: Every summer, parents start asking some version of the same question: how can we keep the kids learning when school disappears? Sure, there are worksheets, apps, and activities focused on everything from long division to Longfellow, but what most young people need in summer isn’t more instruction—it’s permission to stay curious. And this year, space may be giving us exactly that. Between excitement around the Artemis II mission, NASA’s breathtaking new images from deep space, and a summer full of exhibitions and conversations about exploration of universes near and far, space is suddenly everywhere again. And kids are paying attention. Recently, my family listened to The New York Times Daily podcast episode where children asked Artemis II astronauts questions about going to the moon. Some were delightfully kid-specific: Do astronauts have to eat broccoli? Others were profound: Why are we spending billions of dollars looking at space when people here on Earth are struggling? What struck us most wasn’t the answers–we expect modern scientists traveling around the moon on a research mission to have profound respect for Earth, for science, and for humanity– it was the questions kids asked. Kids can move effortlessly from asking about astronaut food to wondering whether space exploration is morally worthwhile. As we listened to the kids’ questions, we found ourselves asking our own: Why the moon? Why now? What can images from distant galaxies teach us about our own planet? articles.text: It has been a season of growth, grit, and milestone performances for the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. The season concluded with the 2026 NorCal Interscholastic Cycling League’s High School Championship on May 16-17 at Six Sigma Winery in Lower Lake, where the team camped, barbecued, and celebrated the growth of the riders, especially the seniors on the team. This year’s course was three miles with an elevation gain of 450 feet. Jasper Schuetz concludes high school career Jasper Schuetz, co-captain of the Piedmont MTB Team, concluded his high school racing career by finishing fifth of 76 riders in the Varsity Boys’ race with a time of 1:26:17.29 on the fourlap course Schuetz began his journey with the team in 8th grade. Over the past four years, he swept the Freshman category in his first season, winning every race and the Championship. As a sophomore, he led JV1 in the East Bay/ Central League and 4th in the NorCal. And during his senior year, he was the Varsity Leader for the East Bay/Central League. As an independent rider, Jasper has taken on some of the most demanding events in the sport: the Grasshopper Series Junior title, back-to-back 4th place finishes at Sea Otter Classic Under 18, U18 1st Place Winner at Lost and Found (100 miles), U18 1st Place at Heart of Gold (73 miles and 10,000 feet of climbing), winner of the Wente 2-person relay in 2025, and U18 2nd Place at the Rad Dirt Fest in Trinidad, Colorado (113 miles). He is also a brand ambassador for Pas Normal Studios in San Francisco. On May 30th, he competed in the 2026 Life Time Unbound Jasper Schuetz, a Piedmont High School senior, finished the Life Time Unbound Gravel 200-mile race in Emporia, Kansas in less than 12 hours on May 30, 2026. Gravel race in Emporia, Kansas. This 200-mile race is widely regarded as the world’s premier gravel event. This year’s edition had brutal weather making an already punishing course even more relentless. Jasper rode 11 hours and 50 minutes to place 53rd overall in a field of 1,251 riders, and also 14th in the Male 16-29 category. The 206-mile ride included heavy thunderstorms, pounding rain and wind, thick mud, muggy conditions, and 6,700 feet of elevation gain. He will return from the Unbound race to graduate from Piedmont High School. This fall, Jasper heads to Cal Poly San Luis Obispo to study Engineering and join the Mustangs Cycling Team. Zachary Carter, a Piedmont High School sophomore, pushes through the Finish Line at the NiCA Norcal Championships at Six Sigma Winery in Lor Lake JV2 girls’ race in sixth of 47 with a time of 1:02:36.31 on the twolap course. She had a standout performance at the NICA NorCal Championships this season, having retained the leader jersey and taking 1st place for JV2 for the East Bay/Central League. Mina Herrgott and Olivia Bailey were also in the race, finishing ninth and 14th with respective times of 1:04:57.40 and 1:07:25.17. Herrgott and Bailey are NICA GRiT Ambassadors — NICA’s program dedicated to recruiting and retaining more girls in interscholastic cycling. These three sophomores continued to race the weekend after Championships at the Ukiah Mendo Gravel Epic, part of the Grasshopper Adventure Series. Josephine, Olivia, and Mina entered the Medium Course together in the Junior Women 16-18 category, and swept the podium. This ride on a 34-mile course with nearly 3,897 feet of climbing took just a little over 3 hours. Zachary Carter: Co-Captain on the Rise Zachary Carter, a sophomore and incoming Team Co-Captain, has emerged as one of the most exciting developing racers in the program. Carter finished the JV1 Boys’ Division 2 race in 16th of 78 in 1:14:42.23 over his three-lap race. This season, Zachary earned podium finishes and demonstrated the kind of consistency and drive that points to big things ahead. He has been a leader on and off the bike, and his trajectory as a racer is strong in the years to come. Emilio Roberts raced in the freshman boys’ D2 event, clocking 55:57.88 over two laps to finish 31st of 80. Chase Mellers was 38th in 58:33.63. The 32nd annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek will be on view June 13 through August 9, featuring over 80 sculptures from 42 artists. The event is the nonprofit’s longest-running annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. A range of returning local artists, as well as newcomers, are participating this year. Sculpture in the Garden also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/. ®

articles.text: Visit the Randall Museum in San Francisco next month and participate in a variety of kidfriendly science, engineering and art activities, ranging from free, drop-in activities to ticketed workshops. The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages. Every Saturday morning in June, young visitors and their caretakers can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Both have been rehabilitated by museum staff and offer a glimpse into California’s wildlife. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. Drop-in art classes are offered every Saturday between 1 p.m. and 3:30 p.m., appropriate for children ages 4 and older. A different activity is featured each week. Visit https://randallmuseum. org to learn more. A young visitor views an exhibit at Randall Museum.

articles.text: Free admission for kids through summer Filoli Museum and historical estate debuted an exhibition, “Creating Home,” on May 30, that explores themes of home, habitat and belonging. The exhibit will be on view throughout the summer and spans the historic estate’s gardens, house, redwood groves and natural campus. It features interactive installations, storytelling experiences and educational programming designed to encourage visitors to engage with the people, animals and trees that shape the property. The centerpiece of the exhibition is a large-scale outdoor installation by California artist Jayson Fann. Constructed from naturally found wood and organic materials, the sculptural works are inspired by bird nests, tree hollows and other natural shelters found throughout the landscape. “This summer at Filoli is all about exploration, discovery, and inspiration,” Kara Newport, president and CEO of Filoli, said in a press release. “With ‘Creating Home,’ guests will uncover interactive installations inspired by the animals, trees, and stories that shape Filoli’s landscape, while ‘Kids Go Free’ makes it even easier for families to spend the day outside together. From the gardens and historic house to the redwoods and trails, there’s something around every corner waiting to spark curiosity and joy.” The exhibition opens alongside Filoli’s Kids Go Free summer promotion, aimed at encouraging family visits throughout the season. Starting May 30, children up to age 14 get in free with every full-price adult ticket. Tickets must be reserved in advance online, and the offer is valid for daytime admission only. In addition to Fann’s outdoor installations, visitors will find immersive room displays inside the historic house highlighting the stories of staff members who helped shape Filoli. Other interactive elements include projected ballroom dance lessons, listening stations featuring imagined historic conversations and opportunities for guests to share family stories. Storytelling signage, daily staff talks and family-focused educational activities will also highlight local wildlife, notable trees and the ecosystems found across the estate. “I have worked with naturally found wood since early childhood, growing up along the Platte River,” Fann said. “This lifelong practice of listening deeply to the land, shaped by flowing water, wind, lightning, thunder, and the rhythms of the landscape, continues to inform my approach to nest building. In Creating Home, these elements come together to remind us that building, belonging, and care all arise through relationships with the world around us.” For more information, visit https://filoli.org/.

Berkeley Playhouse’s staging reimagines the musical’s traditional junkyard setting as a long-forgotten vintage theater, transforming the stage into what organizers describe as a dreamlike spectacle featuring dance styles including ballet, tap, jazz and acrobatics. “For my tenth birthday my family brought me on a day trip to San Francisco. Eliot and Andrew Lloyd Webber than an old theater, once forgotten but with the spark of pure magic still alive within it,” she added. articles.text: This summer, the Bay Area will resonate with extraordinary music as the Golden Gate International Choral Festival welcomes over 450 choristers, adjudicators, and chaperones from around the globe for a week of breathtaking performances, cultural exchange, and artistic excellence. The opening concert is on Monday, July 13, at 4 p.m. at the Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church. Taking place July 13–18, 2026, and hosted by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, the Festival stands as one of the world’s most celebrated gatherings of young singers. Under the leadership of Artistic Director Eric Tuan, internationally recognized as one of the world’s premier youth choir conductors, the Festival promises performances of cultural significance and emotional power. “The Golden Gate Festival is a place where young people from around the world build bridges between cultures,” says Tuan. “Even in a deeply divided world, the Festival offers us the chance to connect through the universal language of music, bringing our unique cultures and voices together to create international harmony. Children who sing together cannot build walls or create conflicts. They know in a deep, visceral way that what unites us is far greater than what divides us.” The Golden Gate Festival remains the only opportunity in the United States for children’s and youth choirs to meet and compete on an international stage. This year, visiting choirs will travel from the Philippines, Georgia, Austria, Catalonia, Poland, Finland, Estonia, Czechia, and across the United States, creating a vibrant and diverse cultural exchange that defines the Festival experience and fosters lasting global friendships. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is a nationally recognized choral organization dedicated to artistic excellence, education, and community engagement. Through transformative musical experiences, PEBCC inspires young singers to achieve the highest levels of musicianship while fostering global understanding. Readers can purchase tickets on Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s website: https://www. piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.

articles.text: Kajetán, the Czechia choir The Czech choir Kajetán is participating in the Golden Gate International Choral Festival. The children‘s opera choir of Josef Kajetan Tyl’s theatre was founded in 2014 in Pilsen, and it is attended by children aged 11 to 19. The choir’s spotlight performance is on July 15 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The choir conductors are Anna-Marie Lahodová and Zuzana Kuncová, accompanist is Olga Cviková. They learn not only the basics of singing and vocal techniques, but also develop aesthetically and socially. The choir‘s repertoire includes children‘s parts of operas as well as classical choral compositions, which the choir performs at various cultural events and concerts. Currently, the children sing in productions of Hansel und Gretel, Špalíček, The Bartered Bride, The Kiss, Czech Christmas Mass, and The Nutcracker. In 2023, Kajetán achieved remarkable success in several choir competitions. Firstly, the children’s choir competition Porta musicae, where Kajetan won the Gold Medal, became the winner of the category and also became the absolute winner of the whole contest. In the Franz Schubert Choir Competition & Festival held in Vienna, Kajetán was awarded a Golden Diploma level VI. At the International Choir Competition Festival of Songs in Olomouc, Kajetán made a significant impact by clinching victory in both of its entered categories, receiving the audience award, and achieving the pinnacle of success by winning the Grand Prix, thereby becoming the absolute winner of the 50th edition of this contest. In 2024, Kajetán achieved further international recognition by winning 1st, 2nd, and 3rd places at the prestigious Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod. In 2025, Kajetán continued its success by becoming the Grand Prix winner in the children’s choir category at the European Choir Games & Grand Prix of Nations in Aarhus, Denmark, and also received three additional gold medals in other festival categories. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 3, 2026 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Captain Fantastic – an Oscar-nominated film By Chris Honoré Oscar-nominated Captain Fantastic, written and directed by Matt Ross, finds a complex and revelatory sweet spot and expands on it. In so many ways this film is sublimely poetic while remaining firmly grounded as it probes the many facets of what it means to be a parent. It is also an engaging and captivating character study. At the film’s center is Ben, portrayed by Viggo Mortensen, a gifted, nuanced actor who inhabits Ben completely as he grapples with all of the subtle and overt challenges of being a single parent to six very independent children. But their collective lives are not lived in a suburban two-story home somewhere on the West Coast; rather, home is a camp of sorts, nestled in the verdant forest of the Pacific Northwest. They live in a place apart, off the grid, and their existence, that of the children, mirrors the values of their father. He strives to instill in them a fearlessness toward life, to think for themselves, to let their minds engage in the seminal questions of purpose and existence, questions that dominate their days. With the urging of Ben they fill their evenings as they search for answers in books and more books, from literature to philosophy to biology and history; his oldest son, Bodevan (George McKay), has recently decided he is a Maoist, a declaration that prompts a smile from Ben. A scene from Captain Fantastic with Viggo Mortensen, George MacKay, Annalise Basso, Samantha Isler, Shree Crooks, Nicholas Hamilton, and Charlie Shotwell As well, they are schooled to be survivalists, to engage in extreme rock climbing, hunting, hand-to-hand combat, and they find together a harmony and web of support and concern that so often eludes families surrounded by the trappings and distractions of a consumer-driven pop culture saturated with electronics. What fractures this harmony is the death of their mother in a hospital in New Mexico where she was taken for treatment. The children, at first devastated, argue strongly, against the wishes of Ben, that they want above all else to attend their mother’s funeral. Ben fears the journey could have unintended consequences; however, he finally relents. And suddenly these children of the forest, with all of their attendant skills, are confronted with a culture steeped in all that Ben has attempted to shield them from: television, Gameboy, Walmart and a funeral, organized by their grandparents (Frank Langella and Ann Dowd), a religious ceremony that they know is against the wishes of their mother. This immersion is both humorous and revealing and for most of the children jaw-dropping. These are not feral children, but neither are they, for all of their resilience, children of this century. Painfully, gradually, Ben is faced with a truth that he has tried to avoid: while his children are supremely prepared for a good part of life, they are also woefully lacking in so many other aspects of what it means to live in a complete world. His didacticism – embedded with his values and convictions and love – has been his gift to them. But the revelation that haunts him is that their lives have been unexpectedly truncated, their prism while wide and encompassing and rich has also been too narrow. Perhaps Ben has loved his children too much. Captain Fantastic is a beautifully crafted film, a story that is life-affirming and lovely, thanks in great part to exceptional writing by Ross and a fine ensemble of actors, all wonderful. Surprisingly, this story comes along at a time when so much of our lives can feel disjointed, and our values seemingly inadequate to the issues that confront us. In essence, our contemporary grid can sometimes seem frayed, at times empty and unfulfilling. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group has visited Piedmont’s Heritage Trees many times over the years, but last Wednesday’s walk was special. An excellent crowd of 41 walkers and three K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra for a tour of the city’s notable Heritage Trees, led by walker and Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup and guest leader Dave Johnson, who also serves on the Park Commission. Dave was UC Berkeley’s campus landscape architect for many years. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council on a recommendation from the Park Commission. More than 30 trees have since been designated as Piedmont’s “Heritage Trees.” The program aims to recognize noteworthy, distinctive trees in city parks and open spaces, encourage residents to visit those spaces, and promote the study of nature. After Jack’s introduction, Dave referenced his Cal predecessor, Jim Horner, and Jim’s book Trees of the Berkeley Campus, which covers every tree the group would see in Piedmont. To the walkers’ delight, Jim joined them later in the morning. Dave also noted that Piedmont has 8,000 street trees and provides trees from its corporation yard, at no cost, for the public spaces in front of residents’ homes. The first Heritage Trees were easy to find: the grove of ten surrounding the Exedra Plaza. A hybrid of two North American poplars, their Latin name is Populus nigra italica and they are commonly called “Highland Poplars.” These are relatively short-lived trees, Dave said, and will eventually have to be replaced. Behind the Exedra in upper Piedmont Park, the group admired a well-known Coast Live Oak. This native species is one of the most common in Piedmont, and this particular tree is a local icon that families have used for photos for decades. Dave pointed out that it is leaning and twisting toward sunlight, with one big branch essentially holding up the entire tree. At the Piedmont Community Hall, the walkers noted the Yulan magnolia in the front circle — a deciduous species native to central and eastern China that produces stunning white spring flowers. Just above it, in the parking lot, stands the Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s Holiday Tree; the color at the top of such trees, Dave explained, indicates how healthy they are. The group passed the Tea House and climbed the Highland Guilford Steps, a grand entrance to the park’s Cherry Walk. Surrounding Heritage Trees there include Japanese maples and a grove of Prunus Akebono flowering cherries, whose beauty and seasonal importance Dave and Jack discussed. Emerging from the park, the walkers went down Highland and Guilford Avenues to a set of hidden steps leading to Hazel Lane. A highlight was a stop to view one of Piedmont’s largest Sequoia sempervirens — Coast Redwoods — which made a natural backdrop for a group photo. On Wildwood Avenue, the group examined the colorful Autumn Blaze Maples lining both sides of the street. Pointing to the grass strips in front of homes, Dave asked the walkers to imagine three feet of water atop one foot of grass — the amount needed to keep it green for a year in Piedmont. In California desert cities, it takes 15 to 20 feet. Dave and Jack also explained that California has passed a law prohibiting cities from using potable water to irrigate decorative, “non-functional” turf starting January 1, 2027 — grass that serves no recreational or community purpose, such as street medians, strips between sidewalks and streets, and areas around commercial parking lots. articles.text: With summer vacation rapidly approaching, many dog owners are planning trips that include their furry friends. Traveling with your dog can be exciting, but stressful as well. Many dogs simply aren’t trained in the skills necessary for travel and end up causing problems for owners or negatively impacting others in public. Bad experiences with untrained dogs may even cause businesses and rentals to revoke pet access altogether. The following are a few essential behaviors every traveling dog should know to keep trips stress free and fun. In any dog training situation, safety should be the first priority. One common issue arises in doorways. Teaching your dog to “wait” at doors is essential for preventing bolting into heavy foot traffic or out of hotel rooms. The same rule applies when exiting the car to avoid dangerous situations in parking lots or unfamiliar areas. Another especially useful command is “place,” which asks your dog to go to a bed or mat and remain there calmly. articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers a great movie in a comfortable setting, with a lively discussion to follow. The Flix Fest June selection is Before Sunrise, a beautifully scripted 1995 romantic drama written and directed by Richard Linklater. pages.text: Wednesday, June 3, 2026 23 Don’t leave home without it: training your dog for hotels, rentals, and roadtrips By Sierra Berrick With summer vacation rapidly approaching, many dog owners are planning trips that include their furry friends. Traveling with your dog can be exciting, but stressful as well. Many dogs simply aren’t trained in the skills necessary for travel and end up causing problems for owners or negatively impacting others in public. Bad experiences with untrained dogs may even cause businesses and rentals to revoke pet access altogether. The following are a few essential behaviors every traveling dog should know to keep trips stress free and fun. In any dog training situation, safety should be the first priority. One common issue arises in doorways. Teaching your dog to “wait” at doors is essential for preventing bolting into heavy foot traffic or out of hotel rooms. The same rule applies when exiting the car to avoid dangerous situations in parking lots or unfamiliar areas. Another especially useful command is “place,” which asks your dog to go to a bed or mat and remain there calmly. This behavior is invaluable in hotel A young collie rides safely in her own seat during a roadtrip. rooms, cafés, and pet-friendly restaurants. Crate training is another must. A crate provides a safe, familiar space in new environments, helping reduce anxiety and prevent destructive behaviors. Car safety matters too! Dogs should be comfortable riding in a crate or secured in their own seat with a canine seatbelt rather than climbing on the driver or moving freely around the vehicle. Public manners are equally important when traveling with dogs. Loose leash walking in crowded areas, “leave it” or “off” for avoiding dangerous items on the ground, and a focus cue such as “watch” can make outings far more enjoyable. Keeping your dog’s attention on you helps when navigating busy sidewalks, parks, hotel lobbies, or passing other dogs. A few additional skills can make traveling significantly easier. Teaching your dog to potty on cue with a phrase like “hurry up” can help prevent accidents and keep long travel days on schedule. Dogs should also understand that excessive barking is unacceptable, especially in hotel rooms and cars. Crating your dog often helps prevent barking and anxiety in unfamiliar environments. With these skills, your dog can become a delightful travel companion. The key to successful travel with dogs is creating a safe, respectful, and enjoyable environment for everyone involved — including you, your pup, and those around you. Be sure to understand the difference between traveling with a pet versus a service dog to avoid legal confusion, and take time to ensure both you and your dog are comfortable before embarking on long trips. With consistency and practice, you and your dog can become lifelong explorers together. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: The Hella Chenin Wine Festival sold out for the second year. In a wine world often dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, one Bay Area festival is making the case that Chenin Blanc deserves its moment in the spotlight. The second annual Hella Chenin Wine Fest in Berkeley drew wine lovers, sommeliers, and curious newcomers to Hammerling Wines for a lively celebration of one of the wine world’s most versatile grapes. The soldout event featured more than 70 Chenin Blanc wines from California, Oregon, South Africa, Australia, and France. Founded by Peter Andrews of Culture Wine Co., Josh Hammerling of Hammerling Wines, and Marty Winters and Alex Pitts of Maître de Chai, Hella Chenin was created with a simple mission: give Chenin Blanc “the spotlight it deserves.” The festival transformed Berkeley’s industrial West Side into a vibrant gathering place filled with tasting tables, live music, oysters, and conversations about old vines, natural winemaking, and the future of California wine. Consumers mingled directly with winemakers in a relaxed, walk-around format that felt more neighborhood block party than formal tasting. For many attendees, the appeal of Chenin Blanc lies in its remarkable range. The grape can produce crisp, mineral-driven whites, rich textured wines, sparkling bottlings, and even sweet dessert wines. At Hella Chenin, tasters sampled everything from lean, Loire-inspired styles to sun-soaked California expressions. The event also carried a charitable mission, with proceeds benefiting CHIRLA, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights. Organizers say they hope Hella Chenin becomes an annual tradition — and judging by this year’s sold-out turnout, Bay Area wine lovers are ready to keep the party going. There were many, many outstanding wines poured at the tasting. At the end of the day the following wines were the standouts – the best of the best of Chenin Blanc. • 2024 Chateau D’ Epire Savennieres The Savennieres region of the Loire Valley is the home to some of longest-lived white wines in the world. I have bottles of this very cuvee in my cellar that are 20 years old and still fresh and vibrant. The 2024 D’Epire offers a clear, fresh and aromatic bouquet of ripe pears and flint stone notes. Medium bodied and very elegant on the palate, this is a perfectly ripe and juicy Chenin with a firm and persistent structure and a very long finish. Stick this in your cellar and forget about it for a few years and you will be richly rewarded. The atmosphere was festive at the West Berkeley tasting.

This is well balanced with peach and mango on the entry, with well-judged acidity and a satisfying, spice box finish that lingers. With six years of bottle age this wine is still vibrant and fresh and has many years ahead of it. • 2025 Teffy Chenin Blanc Jurassic Park Vineyard The Teffy Chenin Blanc has a superb nose rich in personality with ripe melon, papaya and honeysuckle that is very intense and shows stupendous clarity. The palate is crisp and very well balanced with grapefruit and crisp apple flavors, with hints of almonds towards the long finish that urges you to take another sip. This is simply excellent. articles.text: Happy June! Two of the things that make Piedmont such a beautiful town are its lovely, well-tended parks and the trees that line so many of its streets. Piedmont’s Heritage Tree Program recently celebrated its eighth year. Every spring, a few of Piedmont’s most beloved trees get a little extra recognition. The City’s Heritage Tree Program invites residents to nominate trees in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces for a formal designation honoring their aesthetic, educational, or historical significance. This year, three new trees joined the growing roster: a Coast Live Oak in Upper Dracena Park, Ginkgo street trees on King Avenue, and a Redwood in lower Dracena Park. Their selection was announced at the city’s annual Arbor and Earth Day Celebration on April 23rd at Community Hall, where nominees were recognized and received a limited-edition Heritage Tree lapel pin. The program was established in 2018 by the City Council on a recommendation from the Park Commission. With this year’s additions, 37 trees or tree groups have now earned the designation. The list includes the Evergreen Dogwoods that bloom each spring in front of City Hall and the Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s holiday tree. An interactive map of all designated Heritage Trees is available at piedmont.ca.gov/Heritage Trees. MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: One of the biggest misconceptions I see is homeowners assuming that once they retire, qualifying for a traditional mortgage becomes difficult or impossible. In many cases, the opposite is true. Over the past decade, lenders have become much more flexible in how they view investment, trust, and retirement assets. For homeowners over 59½, money held in IRAs or retirement accounts can often be used to generate qualifying income…even if they are no longer working full-time. That can open doors that many people assume are closed. I increasingly see this helping homeowners buy before selling, renovate, build ADUs, or help family members financially without relying on expensive private financing. Many retirees are far more ‘mortgage-qualified’ than they realize - they just have not been shown how the rules have evolved.

Native trees such as the Coast Live Oak and Coast Redwood sustain a rich biodiversity of insects, caterpillars, butterflies, pollen, and nuts that feed local birds and wildlife.
